newsitem.title: USA: Report to Texaco clears company of one racial slur.
newsitem.headline: Report to Texaco clears company of one racial slur.

text.p: Tapes of Texaco officials' conversations purportedly studded with racial epithets show the men did not use the most offensive term cited in a suit against the oil company, Texaco said on Monday.
In a report to Texaco, which hired him as an independent investigator, former Assistant U.S. Attorney Michael Armstrong says the word "nigger" never figures on the tapes.
News of the tapes' existence was announced last week as part of a federal investigation into allegations that Texaco destroyed documents to protect itself in the racial discrimination suit.
Texaco released Armstrong's report on Monday, noting that it addressed only the allegations of racist remarks and reached no conclusions about claims that documents were destroyed.

In prefacing the report, Texaco Chairman Peter Bijur said that although the findings cleared the company of the most disturbing comment alleged in the suit, it "does not change the categorically unacceptable context and tone of those conversations."

Armstrong says the phrase "black jelly beans" was used but probably not as a racial epithet. He says the phrase more likely referred to, and was repeated from, a speech given by a leading lecturer on racial diversity, R. Roosevelt Thomas Jr.

Thomas, former president of the American Institute for Managing Diversity at Morehouse College in Atlanta, confirmed he used the analogy of different-coloured jelly beans in his addresses to corporations, Armstrong's report says.

It says the tapes show that two other allegations in the suit -- that the executives criticised black employees for sitting during the national anthem and celebrating Kwanzaa -- are probably accurate.

The tapes surfaced as part of legal proceedings after six black employees sued Texaco in 1994. They claimed the company had systematically discriminated against them in promotions and fostered a hostile environment since early 1991, if not earlier.
The recordings were turned over by Richard Lundwall, who made them as a senior coordinator for personnel services in Texaco's finance department. The company dismissed Lundwall in August.
Armstrong obtained the original tapes from the FBI after duplicates proved to be of poor quality and made new copies, which were enhanced to clarify the sound and remove background noise.
